case.label: C
case.text: An IAM SAML identity provider plus roles in each account also gives short-term credentials from the existing IdP, and some teams already run such a broker; but building and running a custom broker across 12 accounts is clearly more overhead than IAM Identity Center with permission sets, and the CLI single sign-on requirement points to Identity Center. The customer mobile app is a deliberate distractor toward D (Cognito is customer identity), not a second answer.

case.label: D
case.text: D also uses an identity pool with the user pool as provider and gives temporary credentials, so it meets the functional need; it loses only on MOST securely, because every customer could write to every other customer's prefix. The per-identity-ID prefix in C is the least-privilege design. A fails because Amazon S3 does not authorize requests by a Cognito user pool token. Minor note: the stem says 'a prefix for that customer' without saying it is keyed by identity ID, but C defines the prefix that way and nothing in the stem conflicts.

case.label: D
case.text: AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a forest trust also lets WorkSpaces users sign in with on-premises credentials, and the trust does not copy user accounts, so 'accounts remain only in the on-premises directory' still holds. It loses on LEAST operational overhead: a second managed domain plus trust configuration versus a proxy (AD Connector) that only forwards requests to the reachable domain controllers. C fails because Simple AD does not support trusts.

case.label: B
case.text: A phased migration might seem to want both directories side by side, so keeping AD Connector and adding Okta looks gentle; but IAM Identity Center has one identity source at a time, so B is not possible, and the stem says all workforce identities move to Okta. E fails because a Cognito user pool is not an identity source for IAM Identity Center; A fails on overhead across 30 accounts.

case.label: C
case.text: C is the right answer to the twin question about engineers, and a rushed reader who sees 'Organizations' and 'SAML 2.0 identity provider' in the shared first sentences may pick it; but the requirement is customer sign-in with Google and S3 uploads, which is customer identity (Cognito user pool federated with Google plus an identity pool for temporary credentials). An identity pool with Google as a direct provider would also work, but it is not offered, so D stands alone.

answers.flag: B is defensible: creating an organization and an organization instance of IAM Identity Center with the managed directory as identity source is the AWS-recommended workforce pattern and a one-time setup, and the stem gives no constraint against creating an organization, so a careful candidate can argue B over the Directory Service access URL; the key depends on reading 'does not use AWS Organizations' as a constraint and on knowing that an account instance (C) cannot assign permission sets for AWS account access.

case.label: B
case.text: B meets every requirement (directory credentials, console access, no IAM users) and is what AWS recommends for workforce access to the AWS Management Console. The single account simply becomes the management account and can still receive permission set assignments. The extra work is one CreateOrganization call and enabling Identity Center, which is small, so 'LEAST operational overhead' does not clearly separate B from D's access URL plus role assignment, and D's console access through Directory Service is a less common, older pattern that some candidates will not consider.

case.label: C
case.text: C is the LEAST-overhead answer in the twin WorkSpaces question, with the same stem opening, so a candidate who pattern-matches 'domain controllers reachable from the VPC' will choose AD Connector; but Amazon RDS for SQL Server Windows Authentication does not work through AD Connector. RDS for SQL Server can also join a self-managed Active Directory directly, which would beat A on overhead, but that option is not offered, so among the four options A is the only one that works.

case.label: C
case.text: A one-way trust looks like the least-privilege choice, and for many AWS services a one-way trust from AWS Managed Microsoft AD to the on-premises forest is enough; but IAM Identity Center needs a two-way trust to read users and groups in the trusted forests. B fails because IAM Identity Center accepts only one identity source, and D adds a migration project the stem does not ask for.

case.label: B
case.text: B uses the same Cognito user pool with the customers' SAML providers and the same authenticate-cognito action; it differs only in the listener. A candidate could think a separate plain listener is easier to add, but the authenticate action needs an HTTPS listener, so B fails. D fails because IAM Identity Center is workforce identity with one identity source, not per-customer federation for an internet application; A needs custom SAML validation code.

case.label: B
case.text: The assignment is made to a group, so a candidate may expect a mirrored IAM group in the member account with the policy attached; but IAM Identity Center provisions the permission set as one IAM role (name prefix AWSReservedSSO_) that members of the group assume, and it creates no IAM groups or IAM users.

case.label: D
case.text: A user pool group with an IAM role does lead to temporary AWS credentials, and it is the feature the company may use after it adds sign-in; but group roles apply only to users who signed in to the user pool (and still need an identity pool to get credentials), so they cannot serve players who have not signed in. Guest access with the unauthenticated role is the only option for those players.

case.label: D
case.text: A Lambda authorizer that validates user pool tokens also restricts the API to signed-in users and gives more control; it loses only on LEAST development effort, because the COGNITO_USER_POOLS authorizer validates the tokens with no custom code. A filters by IP address, not by sign-in; B creates IAM users for customers.
